newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Security summit, rows apart, pledges peace.
newsitem.headline: Security summit, rows apart, pledges peace.

text.p: Leaders from North America and Europe on Tuesday pledged a new age of security and peace for all in the 21st century, but the Lisbon summit was marred by friction over NATO enlargement, Belarus and Serbia.

Leaders of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) agreed to respect democracy and human rights, and backed more arms control and an end to confrontation on the continent where two world wars started.

"We are determined to learn from the tragedies of the past and to translate our vision of a cooperative future into reality by creating a common security space free of dividing lines," the final summit declaration said.

The OSCE, sometimes accused of spouting lofty ideals, scored a notable success at the summit by agreeing to adapt a 1990 arms reduction pact to reflect a post-Cold War Europe no longer divided by military alliances.
Heads of state and government agreed to develop the idea of a security model for the 21st century, rooted in the principle that no nation's security should be threatened by another.
"This is a very important document," John Kornblum, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs, said.

"Given the history of destruction and warfare on this continent over the past 100 years, ...nations will draw on the tools of solidarity of others to make sure they are secure," Kornblum told a news conference.
But the summit was not free of its diplomatic wrangles.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin underscored Moscow's opposition to NATO plans to take in countries such as Poland and Hungary by the year 2000, raising the spectre of new division lines spreading across Europe.

President Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus drew open criticism from several leaders over his autocratic rule, while Azerbaijan and Armenia rowed publicly over the political stalemate in Nagorno-Karabakh.

Chernomyrdin failed to win support to develop the OSCE into a more powerful security body to act as a counterweight to NATO. But one trophy he can carry home is the agreement to update the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, an issue Moscow has been pushing since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
While the final text supported every nation's right to change its security arrangements, Russia will be gratified that the summit issued no endorsement of NATO enlargement.
In a rare rebuke to a participating member, the OSCE told Lukashenko to ensure the freedom of the media, re-establish full democratic procedures and start talking to the opposition.

"(The OSCE) remains deeply concerned about the constitutional situation in Belarus," said a statement issued at the summit by the foreign ministers of Hungary, Switzerland and Denmark, the so-called "troika" which guides OSCE policy.
"(It) urges the government of Belarus to take action without delay to respect its commitment to OSCE norms and principles."
A row between the former Soviet republics of Armenia and Azerbaijan over the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh threatened to block the final declaration, which needed the agreement of all.
The two countries went to war in 1988 over the issue but have since agreed a ceasefire.

In the end, they agreed to put the row to one side but the debates in Lisbon have underlined how difficult it is to resolve ethnic problems and regional conflicts now the East-West divisions of the Cold War have gone.
Western diplomats said Russia had insisted the declaration remove a call for democracy in Serbia, where President Slobodan Milosevic faces mass protests.

Many leaders in Lisbon had expressed concern that Milosevic, now facing an unprecedented challenge to his nine years of autocratic rule, could use force against protesters now thronging the streets of Belgrade and calling on him to quit.
Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, did not attend the summit because its OSCE membership has been suspended.
The last OSCE summit, in Budapest in 1994, collapsed over differences on the NATO issue and the war in Bosnia.

This summit approved a continued role for the OSCE in Bosnia in 1997, working alongside the NATO-led peace force and supervising local elections, which leaders hoped could be held in the first half of the year.
The OSCE's Bosnia operation builds on its role as a monitor of democracy, human rights and arms control. The forum has its roots in a 1975 East-West conference in Helsinki.

Scores of bilateral meetings were held on the fringes of the summit. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and both later said a dispute over ethnic Germans expelled from Czechoslovakia in 1945 would be resolved soon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, whose countries are OSCE observers, met for private talks both described as useful.
Netanyahu told the summit the OSCE could be an example to the Middle East of how to achieve lasting peace.
